Partitioned dependency compilation passes the project configuration to each partition VM through a file in a fixed-name directory under the shared system temporary directory, and the partition trusts what it reads back. Another local user on the same host can exploit this during a mix deps.compile run that uses partitioned compilation. Mix.Tasks.Deps.Partition.server/4 in lib/mix/lib/mix/tasks/deps.partition.ex creates the directory with File.mkdir_p/1, which accepts an existing directory without checking its owner, so a user who created it first can replace the file before client/0 reads it. items.title: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
items.content:
Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action.

Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network.

I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream.

Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout

with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ( how )

The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough.

On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display.

The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself.

Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/ . It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap.

raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot

you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5

23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives

"Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream ).

You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout , doomlite , flappy , pong ).

The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector.

The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops.

items.title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
items.summary: retrocomputing, reversing
items.content:
So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far.

But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s?

Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything.

Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead.

I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies).

I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these drivers on my earlier NT port ran entirely using disk images on a FAT filesystem, due to the requirement for compatibiltiy with existing homebrew loaders that load executables from FAT filesystems, but this would naturally be limited to 4GB images for FAT32, and later versions of classic Mac OS needed more), so for initial testing I just took the “Mac OS ROM” TBXI file and placed it directly on a FAT filesystem as \ppc\bootinfo.txt for OpenBIOS to load it on boot.

So with that I could get the Trampoline running. I decided that I should try and apply as many patches to the image as possible as close to run-time as possible, so mostly untouched existing CD images could be used eventually.

The first issue I had was that the Trampoline makes some assumptions of the physical address space layout that are not true for this system. The physical address of a buffer gets calculated as an invalid address, so I patched that to an address guaranteed to be valid, and also the corresponding code setting up the memory chunk list/page table entries for the kernel.

Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.

Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collective DDoSecrets were marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outlets broke the news that Homeland Security had been hacked.

TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked datasets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.”

In a statement, Bluesky chief operating officer Rose Wang told TechCrunch: “Our Community Guidelines protect people’s safety and privacy by prohibiting the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks. Because the files include the email addresses and phone numbers of individuals, shared without their authorization, we are blocking links to the dataset.”

“When deciding between blocking a link and removing individual posts, we chose to block the links to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary,” said Wang.

In a post on Bluesky, Wang said that the company plans to change the wording on the block message. “We should have changed the wording last night. Changes incoming shortly,” said Wang.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.

“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.

Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.

A search site , dubbed Icepick, made by journalist maia arson crimew no longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” which generally means that the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.

Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.”

items.title: GM Allegedly Spied On Drivers And Sold Their Data, Now It’s Paying A $220M Settlement
items.content:
If you had a suspicion your modern car is spying on you, you’re probably right. Vehicles these days are connected to the Internet of Things, able to feed data back to the cloud in real time. Once it’s there, what happens next may not be something you explicitly agreed to. Now the tide is starting to shift. After allegedly selling data on drivers to third parties without clear consent, General Motors has agreed to a $220 million settlement and terms that aim to limit data collection and establish new, more ethical practices.

So how did we get here? Back in 2024, the New York Times broke the story that GM was allegedly sharing vehicle data with data broker LexisNexis. Data that reportedly included trip distance, instances of speeding, instances of hard braking, and instances of sharp acceleration. Insurance companies could then use a driver’s LexisNexis risk profile to raise rates, and most drivers were completely unaware of this arrangement.

One of the big alleged problems here is that active consent to data-sharing was virtually nonexistent. According to a New York Times writer who owned a GM vehicle and signed up for OnStar’s Smart Driver event monitoring function, “there was no warning or prominent disclosure that any third party would get access to my driving data.” What’s more, the paper reports that “some drivers with vehicles made by G.M. say they were tracked even when they did not turn on the feature — called OnStar Smart Driver — and that their insurance rates went up as a result.”

While it was possible to unenroll from the Smart Driver program without spending hours on the phone, it was effectively a seven-step process for a driver to remove themselves from a program they might not have known they were already in. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this attracted a great deal of scrutiny, to the point where a coalition of 36 Attorneys General brought forward a case.

Oregon was one of the co-leaders behind the coalition, and the complaint in that state was brought forward under alleged “violations of the Oregon Unlawful Trade Practices Act.” As per a statement issued by the Oregon AG office:

Most people who ended up in Smart Driver were enrolled at the dealership when they bought their car, through a single sign-up process that also enrolled them in GM’s OnStar services. In many cases, dealership employees allegedly accepted the terms and conditions on customers’ behalf without their consent.

At the time, GM was aggressively pushing dealerships to sign up as many OnStar customers as possible. Sales employees earned bonuses based in part on how many customers they enrolled in GM’s connected vehicle services, and dealerships were ranked by their enrollment numbers.

The OnStar app also wrongly told over 370,000 drivers they were not enrolled in Smart Driver when they were, and GM was collecting and selling their data the whole time. GM later quietly unenrolled those drivers without telling them about the mistake and left their data in the hands of data brokers and insurers.

That last part seems like an especially egregious ethical violation, as it reads exactly like spying. Collecting data on those who are unaware, denying the collection of data, then quietly stopping monitoring while maintaining said data. Especially since GM’s Smart Driver metrics are likely poor indicators of how safe a driver actually is. As my colleague Jason Torchinsky previously wrote :

Take the “hard braking” metric, for example. It’s treated as a negative, with scores lowering if you have a lot of hard braking incidents. But there are absolutely times while driving where you  want  to brake, and brake hard. If a kid or deer or a kid on a deer or dog or tortoise or whatever bolts out unexpectedly in front of you, a safe driver will apply their brakes, hard. Soft, gradual braking is  not  safe in such a situation, but the data gathering does not appear to take the overall situation into account.

JSON.decode/1 and JSON.decode!/1 convert each integer literal with erlang:binary_to_integer/1 and do not bound its length. items.title: What we know so far about Spain train crash
items.content:
What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash

36 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Watch: What leaked audio reveals about Spain train crash

Two trains crashed south of the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday morning, on the high-speed line to Seville.

At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision, when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda.

It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning have been declared in the country.

Here is what we know about the crash so far.

The crash happened at 08:53 (07:53 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, according to an account given by the Spanish government.

The privately run Iryo train was stationary on the state-run Renfe train barrelled into the back of it at high speed. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown".

The crash caused some carriages to fall down an embankment.

All train traffic on the line was stopped at stations along the route.

Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.

A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.

Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 08:30 on Wednesday morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.

"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre that decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.

That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks about 25km (15 miles) ahead.

Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media between train controllers working in Madrid for a rail infrastructure company in Adif in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move at 08:36 even though another one ahead had stalled.

In one recording, the controller tells the driver of the Renfe train to disconnect and reconnect the LZB mechanism that monitors train speeds, and then resume the journey at normal speed.

"Disconnect and reconnect LZB. Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.

The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."

Young athlete and former minister among victims

Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

Under normal protocols, the driver would be expected to continue moving at a maximum of 40km/h according to their line of sight, and not at normal speed on a track designed for speeds of up to 200km/h.

The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.

In a second audio recording between the driver of the Iryo train in front and the control centre, the driver says the train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda". After some exchanges, the control centre operator tells the driver to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.

items.title: Design the interface for functionality not familiarity
items.summary: mac
items.content:
This blog post is about touch screen Macs, but I’ll start by talking about touch screen cars. Vehicle manufacturers have increasingly replaced physical controls in cars with touch screens, and it hasn’t gone well, because the touch screens frustrate drivers. As a resident of the Upper Midwest who drives wearing gloves in the winter, I suspect that the idea for touch screens came from somewhere warmer than the traditional home of the automotive industry, Detroit. For further reading on the serious, indeed dangerous problems with touch screens in cars, I found a couple of recent articles from Popular Mechanics and The Conversation .

Smartphones have become ubiquitous, bringing ubiquitous familiarity with touch screen interfaces. Nonetheless, a touch screen is not the best interface for all purposes. In the case of cars, familiarity breeds contempt! The introduction of touch screens to smartphones was inspired by the physical limitations of the devices. The largest iPhone ever made, the new iPhone Duo, is still significantly smaller when unfolded than the smallest MacBook. Needless to say, the original 2007 iPhone was tiny compared to a MacBook. Mobile phones with a physical keyboard must have a correspondingly smaller screen, so manufacturers eliminated the physical keyboard to maximize screen size, relying entirely on a touch screen interface, including a software keyboard. In this case, touch screens were well motivated.

Over the years I’ve owned many different computing devices of various sizes; from Apple: iMac, Mac Pro, Mac mini, MacBook Pro, iPhone, iPad. I’ve never once tried to control a Mac by touching its screen, not even absentmindedly. I simply never developed that habit. Many other people, however, when first introduced to a Mac, having only used touch screen computers such as smartphones and tablets, habitually attempt to control the Mac by touching its screen. This habit or expectation is cited as justification by defenders of touch screen Macs. In a Wired interview yesterday, Apple Senior Vice President of Worldwide Marketing Greg Joswiak said, “There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.” In my opinion, such an expectation is a terrible reason to introduce touch screen Macs. The habit of touching Mac screens can be broken and is worth breaking, because for most purposes the traditional Mac interface of a keyboard and indirect pointing device (mouse or trackpad) is so much more powerful and productive than the touch screen of an iPhone or iPad.

Before you cite the ungodly AAPL market capitalization as proof that Joz’s opinion trumps mine, consider how Apple is the same company that gave us howlers such as the trash can Mac Pro, Touch Bar, butterfly keyboard, Liquid Glass, and gave a gold statue to Trump. I’m not even making any claims about the future profitability of touch screen Macs. I just think it’s a poor design.

Ironically, people like me who were introduced to computers before the smartphone era are ridiculed as “resistant to change,” yet I’ve managed to learn how to use iPhones and iPads (the latter without a keyboard), so why can’t people who were introduced to computers during the smartphone era learn how to use Macs? Let me quote from a blog post I wrote earlier this year, If computers are the future, why are computer users expected to be permanently illiterate?

A MacBook Pro is bulkier than an iPhone, can’t fit in your hand or your pocket. That’s a disadvantage. Thankfully, a MacBook Pro has many advantages that outweigh the disadvantages. The larger screen size, the physical keyboard, and the less restrictive operating system allow Mac users to perform the same tasks with vastly greater ease than on iPhone or iPad and, moreover, to perform tasks not even possible on iPhone or iPad. It’s a shame to introduce new users to Mac by telling them to use it in the same way they used their old familiar devices, which are strictly limited by both…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: End of Life: 59 Days, One Patch and the XP Left Behind
items.content:
Fifty-nine days passed between March 14 and May 12, 2017. During that gap, the fix for the flaw WannaCry would exploit was already published by Microsoft, in bulletin MS17-010. People who installed it watched the disaster on TV. People who didn't saw a screen asking for $300 in bitcoin. But one detail gets lost when the story is told quickly: the Windows XP machines had no fix waiting for them. The system had been officially dead since April 2014. Microsoft ended up releasing a patch for it during the attack itself, a rare exception, on a day when British hospitals were cancelling appointments. The National Audit Office later counted 81 of 236 NHS trusts as affected. Those machines weren't caught through carelessness. They were caught because they were somewhere carelessness was no longer even possible. For an attacker, every monthly fix to a still-supported system is a clue. You compare the file before and after the update, see what changed, and learn where the hole was. The technique is called *patch diffing* and it is routine in security research, the good kind and the bad. Now add an older version that shares much of its code with the new one. The vendor fixes the new one, publishes, and the equivalent hole in the old one stays open, with its location practically announced. Code doesn't rot with age. What happens is that the world around it keeps discovering things and it stops receiving answers. The risk rises every month, quietly, without anything changing on the computer. An uncomfortable conclusion follows: the machine that didn't fail in seven years doesn't prove security. It proves nobody has tried yet, or that someone already got in and kept quiet. Python 2 was retired on January 1, 2020. CentOS 7 ended on June 30, 2024. Anyone who works with servers knows retired on the calendar doesn't mean switched off in practice. There's a Python 2.7 script in a scheduled job somewhere, generating a report someone reads on Mondays. There's a VPS running a 2019 CentOS that nobody touches because last time the site went down for forty minutes. And there's that dependency its author stopped maintaining, which three other libraries still pull in. In these cases the risk is rarely a targeted attack. It's more boring: automated scanners sweep the internet looking for known vulnerable versions, without choosing victims. If you run unsupported software, you don't need to be interesting to get caught. You just need to be there. ####
What if the machine isn't on the network? It's the best objection and it carries weight. There is industrial equipment, medical devices, CNC machines whose certified software can't be updated without recertifying the whole device. Isolation is the reasonable answer and often the only one. It only answers part of it. Stuxnet crossed isolated networks in 2010 inside USB sticks. Isolation reduces the attack surface, it doesn't remove it, and the discipline that sustains it (nobody plugs in the vendor's laptop, nobody copies a file by stick) is the kind of rule that dissolves after two years. If isolation is your only defence, treat it as such: real segmentation, a log of what goes in, a plan for the day it fails. Not as a permanent state of rest. The closest case is Windows 10, whose support ended on October 14, 2025. Counting to today, that's 381 days. On June 25, 2026 Microsoft extended its free consumer security-update programme to October 12, 2027, when the end had been set for October 2026. The detail that matters is that the programme isn't automatic. Security fixes only reach a Windows 10 machine that is enrolled in ESU. A PC that never enrolled has received none of the fixes from these months. The extension protects those who signed up, not those who never knew it existed. It's a strange situation. A patch is published for the same version of the system, and some identical machines don't get it because of a settings menu nobody opened. In an inventory of twenty machines there is…

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-109821 📢 Source: EEF 💣 CVSS Score: 6.3 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's URI module allows an attacker who supplies a URL to cause a denial of service through CPU exhaustion. URI.parse/1 converts the port component with String.to_integer/1 in split_authority/1 (lib/elixir/lib/uri.ex) without bounding its length, so a port of up to 1,262,592 decimal digits produces a bignum of that size and a longer one raises SystemLimitError. Rendering the parsed URI back to text (URI.to_string/1, inspect/1, logging, error formatting) converts the bignum with :erlang.integer_to_binary/1, which is quadratic on Erlang/OTP 27, 28 and 29.0: a 400,000-digit port renders in about 2.6 seconds and a 1 MB port in about 18 seconds. Ports above 65535 are also accepted. This issue affects elixir: from 0.5.0 before 1.18.6, from 1.19.0-rc.0 before 1.19.7, and from 1.20.0-rc.0 before 1.20.5. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-30T08:54:07.752Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109821
